subject: brain
topic: Your brain may be losing the ability to distinguish truth from fiction
angle: While misinformation sharing is linked to information overload and cognitive load can hinder the effectiveness of corrections, the evidence shows that the anterior cingulate cortex is specifically involved in the emotional processing and cognitive control of dishonest decisions rather than being degraded by misinformation exposure.
title: The Mechanics of Misinformation

hooks.text: Is your brain losing its grip on reality?
You think your brain is breaking. The evidence says otherwise.
You are letting information overload dictate your beliefs.
A blue light screen in a dark room.
How information overload shapes your choices.

reveal.headline: Your brain does not lose its truth-sensing hardware.
reveal.body: Misinformation does not degrade the anterior cingulate cortex. This area remains active during dishonest decisions. Evidence on this specific degradation is currently mixed.

explain.headline: Cognitive load creates a barrier to truth.
explain.body: Information overload and social media fatigue make it easier to share false news. High cognitive load can make a single correction entirely ineffective.

matters.headline: Your willpower is being outpaced by volume.
matters.body: That may be why you find it harder to spot lies when you are tired. The problem is not a broken brain, but an overwhelmed one.

example.headline: Scrolling through your feed at 11 pm.
example.body: You see a headline that fits your view. You share it instantly. You are tired. Your brain is full. The truth feels like too much work to verify.

question.headline: When was the last time you felt truly certain?

stat.label: the success of a single correction under high cognitive load

claims.text: Deceptive immoral decisions under reputation risk make activity and functional connectivity between the bilateral ACC and left AI increase.
claims.quote: Crucially, deceptive immoral decisions under reputation risk enhanced activity of - and functional connectivity between - the bilateral ACC and left AI, suggesting the need for heightened emotional processing and cognitive control when making immoral decisions under reputation risk.

claims.text: Dishonest decisions are linked to increased activity in the bilateral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and anterior insula (AI).
claims.quote: Dishonest decisions were associated to increased activity in a cortico-subcortical circuit including the bilateral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), anterior insula (AI), left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, supplementary motor area, and right caudate.

claims.text: Cognitive load reduces the effectiveness of corrections to misinformation, with a single correction being entirely ineffective under load.
claims.quote: cognitive load reduced correction effectiveness, with a single correction entirely ineffective under load.

claims.text: Low cognitive ability makes the effect of information strain and information overload on misinformation sharing more pronounced.
claims.quote: cognitive ability moderated and weakened the effect information strain and information overload have on misinformation sharing in such a way that this effect is more pronounced among those with low cognitive ability.

claims.text: Using an infographic reduces cognitive load, which makes people better able to verify false news.
claims.quote: Drawing from processing fluency theory, we propose that an infographic – a visual representation of information – reduces cognitive load, thereby helping people retain and process the necessary information to discern truth from falsehood in health news.

claims.text: Information overload and social media fatigue are linked to sharing misinformation.
claims.quote: Our findings suggest that information overload and social media fatigue are strong predictors of misinformation sharing.

verdict: The sources show that cognitive load and information overload facilitate the spread and persistence of misinformation, but they do not provide evidence that high-frequency exposure to misinformation degrades the brain's ability to activate the anterior cingulate cortex.
caveat: None of the provided sources specifically measure the degradation of the anterior cingulate cortex's error-detection capabilities as a direct result of high-frequency misinformation exposure.
caption:
Information overload makes it harder to tell what is true.

Research shows that while cognitive load hinders the effectiveness of corrections, the brain's hardware for detecting dishonesty remains intact. However, the evidence does not show that high-frequency exposure to misinformation degrades the anterior cingulate cortex.
